feedback.nudge: Two questions per class. Can the chain leave it? And if it comes back, at which times can it come back? The first question separates recurrent from transient; the second separates the two recurrent classes from each other.

explanation:
## The four classes

**$\{1,2\}$.** $1 \to 2 \to 1$ and nothing else; no arrow leaves. It is closed and finite, so it is recurrent (Theorem 3.36(b)). Starting at 1 the chain is at 1 exactly at even times, so $J_1 = \{2,4,6,\dots\}$ and the period is $\gcd J_1 = 2$.

**$\{3\}$.** Both arrows out of 3 leave the class — to 1 and to 4 — so the chain is gone after one step and never returns, because neither $\{1,2\}$ nor $\{4,5\}$ leads back. $\P_3(\text{return to } 3) = 0$, so 3 is transient.

**$\{4,5\}$.** $4 \to 5 \to 4$, and $4 \to 4$. No arrow leaves, so it is closed and finite, hence recurrent. The self-loop at 4 gives $1 \in J_4$, so the period is 1: aperiodic.

**$\{6\}$.** The self-loop keeps the chain at 6, but with probability $\tfrac12$ each step it moves to 3 and is gone. The number of steps spent at 6 is geometric with mean 2, and after that there is no way back. Transient.

## The verdict that cannot happen

"Recurrent but not closed" is impossible, and that is Theorem 3.36(a): **every recurrent class is closed.**

The argument is short and worth knowing. Suppose $C$ is a class, $i \in C$, and $p_{i,j} > 0$ for some $j \notin C$. Then $j \not\to i$ — otherwise $j$ would be in $C$ — so with probability at least $p_{i,j} > 0$ the chain leaves $i$ and never comes back. That makes the return probability strictly less than 1, so $i$ is transient.

Read in the other direction: if you can get out and cannot get back, you are transient. That single sentence decides $\{3\}$ and $\{6\}$ here without any computation.

## The converse needs "finite"

"Every finite closed class is recurrent" is Theorem 3.36(b), and the word **finite** is not decoration. The simple random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ with $p > \tfrac12$ is a single closed class and every state is transient: the chain escapes to $+\infty$ and never returns. In a finite closed class there is nowhere to escape to, so some state must be visited infinitely often, and a class property argument spreads that to all of them.

## Why the classification is the right first move

Every later question in the chapter is a question about one class at a time. Stationary distributions live on recurrent classes; the convergence theorem needs irreducible, aperiodic and positive recurrent, which is three class properties at once; hitting probabilities are computed by asking which closed class the chain ends up in.

For this chain the long-run answer is now immediate: from 3 or from 6 the chain is eventually absorbed into $\{1,2\}$ or $\{4,5\}$ and stays there for ever, oscillating in the first and settling into a stationary distribution in the second.
